evidence.field: 四 entry, graphic history and attributed analyses; PDF p. 1279, printed p. 1264, continued PDF p. 1280, printed p. 1265
evidence.text: The actual headword is 四 in 四部. I inspected both supplied full-page scan images directly. On printed p. 1264, the entry describes Shang forms as four accumulated strokes used directly for the numeral, normalized as 亖, and says they continued alongside forms written 四 in bronze inscriptions from Western Zhou through Han. It dates a separate graph series to Spring and Autumn and reports Shuowen’s ‘image of division into four’ analysis. The continuation on printed p. 1265 attributes to Ma Xulun the proposal that 四 was the original graph of 泗, depicting nasal discharge, then borrowed for ‘four’; the book explicitly says the proposal lacks textual attestation. This is a reported proposal, not an established derivation. The inspected passage names 泗, not 呬. The quoted relevant OCR passage agrees with the pixels; no OCR correction is proposed.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 天津古籍出版社 / 遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692

evidence.source: 全字庫 CNS11643, Taiwan Ministry of Digital Affairs
evidence.field: 字形資訊: current character structure and reading
evidence.text: The official character record gives 四 as U+56DB, lists its indexing radical as 囗 and its IDS as ⿴囗儿, with Mandarin reading sì. This supports a useful current-form description as an enclosing 囗 shape with inner 儿-form strokes. It documents structure and reading, not the historical identity or original function of those shapes.
evidence.title: 字形資訊 - [四] 1-463E - 全字庫 CNS11643

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Center for Chinese Linguistics Character Database
evidence.field: graphic evolution and competing graph-origin interpretations
evidence.text: The record displays bronze forms, including catalogue labels 集成00182 and 集成02837, Chu manuscript forms, and a small-seal form. Its text reports both an interpretation of four horizontal marks as counting rods representing four and a distinct account that a form represented breath issuing from the mouth and was the original graph of 呬, later borrowed for the numeral. The page does not date the listed artifacts or resolve the competing interpretations.
evidence.title: 漢字「四」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 四 entry: formation accounts, numeral use, Shuowen and sound category
evidence.text: The entry reports Xu Zhongshu’s interpretation of oracle forms as four horizontal counting rods representing four. It separately reports a proposal, attributed to Ding Shan and Zeng Xiantong, that a later form was the original graph of 呬, depicting breath from mouth or nose, and was borrowed for the numeral because of sound similarity. It cites 無㠱簋 with the phrase 「王易(賜)無㠱馬亖(四)匹」 as numeral usage. It also transmits Shuowen’s division account and old forms. These are reported interpretations and lexicographic material; the entry does not settle the graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 四

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 亖 under 四; cited Shuowen and historical lexicography
evidence.text: The dictionary records 亖 as a variant under 四 and cites Shuowen’s classification of 亖 as 籀文四, alongside later dictionary and inscription references. This supports a documented graph association, but does not establish that 亖 was the exclusive or earliest numeral graph in every period.
evidence.title: [A00724-001] 亖 (四) - Ministry of Education《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》

evidence.source: Kanji Café, Japanese Kanji Museum and Library
evidence.field: 「なぜ“４”は『四』と書くのか？」, discussion of origin proposals and cited scholarship
evidence.text: This secondary scholarly outreach article distinguishes the 丁山呬/breath proposal from 馬敘倫’s 泗/nasal-discharge proposal and reports 劉洪濤’s preference for the latter. It summarizes Liu’s proposed analysis of certain oracle forms as nose plus flowing liquid, while noting the alleged form was used for a personal or clan name rather than demonstrably for the number or mucus. It is a useful account of disagreement, but the underlying studies it cites were not directly inspected here.
evidence.title: やっぱり漢字が好き。４　なぜ“４”は「四」と書くのか？（下）

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 呬 entry: Shuowen form, gloss and pronunciation category
evidence.text: The separate 呬 record gives the Shuowen analysis 「从口，四聲」 and glosses associated with breathing, gasping and resting. This verifies 呬 as a recorded character with a breath-related lexical history and a traditional account assigning 四 a sound role in 呬. The record does not establish that 四 itself originated as a breath pictograph.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 呬

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 泗 entry: Shuowen composition and recorded meanings
evidence.text: The separate 泗 record transmits Shuowen’s analysis 「从水，四聲」 and describes 泗 as a river name, also recording a mucus/nasal-discharge meaning. This supports treating the book’s proposed 四-to-泗 history as a separately attributed account; the modern/traditional dictionary analysis itself identifies water plus 四 as the formation of 泗 and does not prove the proposed earlier graph history.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 泗

evidence.field: 無㠱簋 object record: date and inscription transcription
evidence.text: The museum dates 無㠱簋 to the middle Western Zhou and transcribes a grant of four horses. Its online transcription renders part of the recipient’s name with question-mark placeholders. It supplies a dated numeral context as reported by the museum, but does not establish an earliest attestation, and the exact numeral graph in the inscription is not independently verified from an image here.
evidence.title: 無㠱簋 - 上海博物館

search_audit.outcome: Search found Taiwan’s official CNS11643 character record, which explicitly lists IDS ⿴囗儿, indexing radical 囗 and Mandarin sì. Opened and inspected that record. This supports present-form structure metadata only, not an ancient component explanation.

search_audit.query: Opened exact character records for 四, 呬 and 泗 at CUHK; Taiwan MOE 亖 variant record; Shanghai Museum 無㠱簋; official Unicode Unihan U+56DB
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the three CUHK records, MOE variant entry and Shanghai Museum object entry. The direct Unicode individual record request returned an internal error and is not used as external reading evidence.

gaps: The source scans support a published description of the Shang numeral form as four accumulated strokes, but an independently inspected primary paleographic catalogue/image tying the exact depicted forms to dated contexts was not consulted in this invocation.

The direct numeral/counting-rod explanation and proposals that a graph associated with 呬 or 泗 was borrowed for ‘four’ remain unresolved. 字源’s 泗 proposal is explicitly marked as lacking textual attestation; it must remain attributed and distinct from the 呬 proposal.
The original spoken name of any proposed depicted breath or nasal-discharge referent is not independently established. Reported sound similarity alone does not prove either proposed graph borrowing.

The museum dates 無㠱簋 to middle Western Zhou and transcribes a four-horse grant, but the online inscription transcription has placeholders in the recipient’s name; the exact rare graph and whether the numeral was written 四 or 亖 were not verified from an artifact image here. This example does not establish earliest priority.
The consulted evidence did not trace dated semantic developments beyond the numeral meaning ‘four’; dictionary gloss lists are not used to infer chronology.

The official Unicode individual record for U+56DB returned an internal error. The Taiwan CNS11643 official record independently provided the modern Mandarin reading sì, so no claim is based on the failed Unicode page.

No local full Unihan or Baxter–Sagart tables were present at the searched repository paths in this checkout; the packet’s supplied row for 四 was not re-presented as external evidence, and no same-system Baxter–Sagart comparison for 呬 or 泗 was verified.
